title: Cautions and Comparisons: How to Burn $1,000,000 a Night
coreMove: Judge money by lifestyle output: if it does not improve what, when, where, or whom, the number is only a louder scoreboard.

exampleSpecs.audience: a revenue director weighing a bonus design
exampleSpecs.stakes: A lucrative award may reward display while leaving the team with less control.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use Mark's Las Vegas spending to separate visible wealth from usable freedom.

exampleSpecs.audience: a parent pricing a year abroad
exampleSpecs.stakes: The family may reject a real option by guessing the cost instead of counting it.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use Julie and Marc's 15-month sailing return to replace intimidation with arithmetic.

exampleSpecs.audience: a chief of staff evaluating a founder's week
exampleSpecs.stakes: The leader may mistake travel perks for freedom while the calendar remains owned by others.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Turn the first-class Las Vegas scene into a calendar control test.

exampleSpecs.audience: an owner deciding whether to delay a sabbatical
exampleSpecs.stakes: A delayed plan may be based on ownership fear rather than real cost.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show the Julie and Marc boat resale logic changing the decision.

exampleSpecs.audience: a store manager deciding how to coach a top seller
exampleSpecs.stakes: The team may celebrate spending cues that teach customers to chase proof instead of fit.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use Mark's cautionary Las Vegas signal to challenge status worship.

exampleSpecs.audience: a designer comparing two income offers
exampleSpecs.stakes: A larger salary may lose once place, rent, and time are counted together.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use Julie and Marc's Paris-versus-voyage math to compare lifestyle output.
